sentences.text: Zaraapelta was a herbivorous ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived in Mongolia during the Late Cretaceous.
This medium-sized dinosaur possessed a robust, pyramid-shaped horn located at the upper rear corner of its skull.
The horn featured a very smooth bone texture along its upper cutting edge, a trait unique among all ankylosaurs.
The cheek area behind the eye socket displays flat bony plates separated by deep grooves, creating a delicate pattern resembling dry mud.
The known fossil record consists of a skull missing the snout tip, with no lower jaw elements found.
No other ankylosaur possesses a squamosal horn with such a smooth upper cutting edge that abruptly transitions to a rough surface on the sides.
The species Zaraapelta nomadis was named and described by Arbour and colleagues in 2014.
The holotype skull was discovered in 2000 by Robert Gabbard in the Gobi Desert near Hermiin Tsav.
The genus name Zaraapelta combines the Mongolian word for hedgehog and the Greek word for small shield to reflect the animal's prickly armor.
The species name nomadis refers to the Nomadic Expeditions travel agency that organized the fossil-hunting trips to Mongolia.
Researchers suggest that the abundance of ankylosaurs like Zaraapelta in the area was due to sufficient vegetation to support multiple herbivore populations.
It is hypothesized that the distinct head ornamentation of Zaraapelta served for species recognition.
Sexual selection is assumed to have played a role in the evolution of Zaraapelta's unique head ornamentation.
Phylogenetic analysis places Zaraapelta as the closest relative to the genus Tarchia.
Cladistic analyses have recovered Zaraapelta as the sister species of Tarchia.
Zaraapelta lived during the Late Cretaceous, specifically the Maastrichtian stage, about 70 million years ago in what is now Asia.

There is a debate regarding whether Zaraapelta is a distinct species or an older individual of Tarchia with shifted bone structures, but authors reject this due to lack of similar ontogenetic changes in other ankylosaurs.
